LITTCII6 AT N6WTON ore SCHDAT SCHOOL TZACHINI, —An interestiog lecture on the :More subjmt was given io Crow-lane school (Congregational Church), on Month:, night, by Mr. Irving Smith, of Brininghat, who ban been. , a lecturer on this And kindred nubjeets for the last 17 years, and seven an ago visited Neston and delivered. lecture. The altered state of e location. the lecturer said, d munded some modification in our methods of teaching. There was 1•. no much talking and too little teaching. The systeto, his experience enabled him to say, which would be found tenet effective, was to find each of the scholars something to do. ' He then proceeded to exemplify. I,y appointing. front a adected class of 20 boys and 20 girls made up of five scholars front the Wesleyan, Primitive Methodist, Baptist, and Congregational schools, a clans secretary, a reprter. emayist, kc., as well as a missionary and money col- lector. The practical working of thin scheme he demon- strated by calling up the bree to read their several reports for the benefit of the andimce, a moderately good one. He then described the difficulties in the way of teaching senior chimes of girl, and Avoca.' the use of oboe into which questions ought be place! for his guidance in finding out their spirito.ll needs; nob he interested the company generally by the suggreice remarks he made throughout the evening. and although the mmlel lesson was almost the , names, the one he gave in Non ton N.fore, as a nroof of the 1 tenacity of fetch public teaching, one of his then class . could recollect distinctly what the points of that losson were, so that to a great extent there is evident proof that much of this kind of teaching is indelible. the more thoughtful of his audience will certainly profit he his ex- perience. There WAS no charge, but a collection was made at the close of the lecture. The Rev. J. Ansa occupied the chair, and said a few words apprecieting the lecturer's labours in the cause of Christianity. The mutre part of the school HU well filled been appreciative audience.

Melling, Ashton) of the estate of Thomas hfillalgton, innkeeper and farmer, Stubehaw. Ashton. a bankrupt. Mr. Melling wee appointed receiver and manager of the estate, but at the first meetmg of creditors afterwauts held, Mr. Henry Rimrner, of Wigan, was appointed trustee, and the latter appli-d to the court for-an order that all papers and moneys belonging to the estate in the hands of the recciver should be handed over to him. Such an order was granted on the 31st of Augnst, but the receiver had not vet paid any money into court, or deposited any of the icieks or Inane., and Mr. Stuart now appl IA for the commitment of the receiver for contempt of the order of the court. —His Honour sant it was a gross ease of contempt of court. Melling had net complied with the order that was on the file, and he made an order for his commitment forthwith.— ! Mr.:heart sug.tested that the order might be suspended for • few days to see if the receiver would deposit the papers. 110.—Hie Honour said he hardly felt disposed to do this. The order had been served up two months ago, and the receiver, by acting thus, had entirely prevented the trustee from reiising the estate. Ho thought this would tree very good example to make. This was the vray in which bank- ruptcy proceedings were delayed and protracted Intimately his honour suspended the commitment until the' . 5520 court day.
